issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Outsider: I am permanently an outsider now
issues.explanation: 'Outsider' is not impossible, but it sits awkwardly with the otherwise accident-focused profile and lacks a clear clinical bridge to the selected triggers, threat items, or coping responses; it reads more like an interpersonal/identity aftermath than the central formulation presented here.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened
issues.explanation: 'Inaction Guilt' is questionable for a life-threatening accident unless the patient had a clear preventable role. As selected, the rest of the profile does not support a responsibility-based narrative strongly enough to make this appraisal cohere.

issues.item: Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
issues.explanation: 'Startle to Touch' is more suggestive of interpersonal assault-related threat than an accident-based threat pattern, and it is not well linked to the selected accident-relevant trigger/avoidance items.

issues.item: Undereating: I avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping
issues.explanation: Undereating is hard to link coherently to the rest of the profile. The active formulation emphasizes a tight Triggers ↔ Threat ↔ Maladaptive Strategies loop centered on accident-related cues and danger responses, but food restriction does not plausibly function as a strategy for the stated triggers or threats and is not supported elsewhere in the profile.

issues.item: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
issues.explanation: Startle to unexpected touch points more toward interpersonal assault-related threat sensitivity than the otherwise accident-focused pattern. With the listed triggers centered on vehicles, illness, and loss of autonomy, this item is not impossible but is notably weakly connected to the rest of the threat profile and trauma type.

issues.item: Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened
issues.explanation: Guilt about not doing more to stop what happened is difficult to reconcile with a life-threatening accident profile unless there is clear evidence of perceived preventability or responsibility. The rest of the appraisals emphasize helplessness and unfairness rather than responsibility, so this item pulls in a different direction and is hard to explain from the provided profile.

vignette:
Sarah had always seen her work in social ministry as a calling, a way to be present for people in the chaos of their lives. Now, chaos was the one thing she could not bear. Six months ago, on a rainy Tuesday afternoon driving back from a home visit, a truck ran a red light and T-boned her sedan. The moments that followed were a blur of shattering glass, the shriek of metal, and a sudden, crushing pressure. She remembers the acrid smell of the airbag and the terrifying inability to move her legs, pinned as she was against the dashboard. In those minutes before the paramedics arrived, a profound sense of helplessness washed over her; her body was not her own, and there was nothing she could do but wait.

In the weeks that followed, this sense of helplessness metastasized into a set of rigid beliefs. She was certain that she could not stop bad things from happening to her. What had occurred was deeply unfair-the other driver was texting, a fact that seemed to get lost in the insurance paperwork-and nothing had been done to right the wrong. This conviction that the world was unjust and she was powerless within it began to poison her perception of safety. Even when friends assured her she was fine, she found it impossible to believe them. This core belief that she was fundamentally unsafe drove a constant, exhausting vigilance. In any new space-a church meeting room, the grocery store-her eyes would immediately dart around, cataloging the exits before she could even sit down.

This pervasive sense of threat is now ignited by the slightest provocation. The screech of tires on a TV show or the sight of mangled cars on the evening news sends a jolt of terror through her. Even feeling physically unwell-a headache, a touch of nausea-becomes a trigger, instantly transporting her back to the feeling of her broken body trapped in the car. Her belief that her body is unreliable makes her exquisitely sensitive to these internal states, turning any physical discomfort into a harbinger of disaster. In response to these triggers, her world has contracted dramatically. The primary casualty has been her work. The thought of getting behind the wheel of a car, or even being a passenger, is intolerable. This avoidance of driving means she has had to transfer all her clients who require home visits, a source of deep shame and a confirmation of her own helplessness.

Her strategies for safety have become a prison. The constant feeling of being under threat compels her to avoid any situation that might escalate it, which for her, now includes almost everything. She avoids driving, situations that put her body under any stress like carrying heavy donation boxes at the ministry, and even tries to avoid relaxing, as letting her guard down feels like an invitation for disaster. These avoidance behaviours, born from her negative appraisals of the world and herself, only serve to amplify her fear. By never driving, she never has the chance to learn that she can be safe in a car, so the imagery of a crash remains a potent trigger. Her avoidance of physical exertion has made her so de-conditioned that normal bodily sensations now feel alien and threatening, reinforcing her belief that her body can't be trusted.

The cycle has become ruthlessly efficient. A trigger, like feeling a cold coming on, confirms her appraisal that her body is unreliable. This appraisal heightens her sense of ambient threat, making her jump at the sound of the office phone ringing. This state of high alert makes avoidance feel not like a choice, but a necessity. She calls in sick, avoiding the stress of work and the perceived danger of her own body, which in turn sensitizes her further to the next trigger. Her life is now circumscribed by these efforts to feel safe, efforts that only reinforce her conviction that she is in constant danger. It was after she had to turn down a promotion because it would require travel between different ministry sites that Sarah finally made an appointment. She feels trapped not by wreckage of metal, but by the architecture of her own fear, and she is desperate, for the first time in a long time, to find an exit.
